description: We're two UNC Chapel Hill undergraduate students with experience in AI/ML and backend development. We want people with UX skills and frontend development experience. Also looking for good public speakers.
summary: EMBER is a fire-safety dashboard and simulator for crewed Moon and Mars habitats, built on NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data. Planned lunar habitats will run at 30% oxygen and 10.2 psi, where materials burn more readily, and at one-sixth gravity, where smoke rises slowly toward detectors. No fire has ever been lit on the Moon, and PSI holds combustion data only at 0 g and 1 g. EMBER brings eight ISS combustion investigations together in one place: it summarizes, compares, and ranks them for the user's habitat and answers questions with citations. A reduced-order simulator calibrated to those experiments then runs AI agents against each other. Red hunts for the fire that is hardest to detect, Blue places detectors to catch it, and a Ghost Flame Auditor flags liquid-fuel fires that look extinguished but keep burning as invisible cool flames, as NASA's FLEX experiment observed. Every number carries a badge showing whether real data measured it, interpolates it, or extrapolates beyond it, so EMBER also maps where NASA's next experiments are needed.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

EMBER helps engineers and researchers reason about fire safety in future lunar and Martian habitats. A user sets up a mission: habitat type (spacecraft, ISS, Moon base, Mars base or pressurized rover), gravity, oxygen fraction, pressure, materials on board and ventilation. EMBER then:

- Summarizes eight NASA ISS combustion investigations (BASS, SAME, DAFT, FLEX, ACME, CFI, SPICE, SLICE) and compares any two side by side.

- Ranks them for the mission by how close their real test conditions are to the user's habitat, filterable by prevention, detection, and suppression.

- Runs a Red vs Blue duel in a 3D habitat: Red searches for the fire that takes longest to detect; Blue optimizes detector positions, ventilation shutoff and suppressant to catch it.

- Runs a liquid-fuel scenario where the Ghost Flame Auditor checks whether a fire reported as "out" could still be burning as an invisible cool flame.

- Answers questions through witness agents, one per investigation, that may only use cited facts.

- Produces an insights report: top risks, recommended fixes, a gravity comparison, a map of untested conditions, and Earth applications.

HOW IT WORKS

The physics is a reduced-order model, not CFD, so it runs fast enough for agents to test hundreds of fires. Smoke and dust move on a 3D grid through ventilation, mixing and buoyancy that scales with gravity. Flame spread is fitted to BASS and BASS-II measurements. Smoke particle size and aging are fitted to SAME-R. Suppression uses FLEX's measured limiting-oxygen values. A two-moment detector model, building on SAME's prototype, separates smoke from regolith dust by particle size. Red and Blue use CMA-ES optimization. An Envelope Guard compares every condition with the nearest real NASA test and badges each result as measured, interpolated or extrapolated. All 60 simulator constants live in one file with their source and status (22 measured, 10 fitted, 28 assumed), and 45 of 48 test conditions were checked row by row against the original papers.

RESULTS (each shown with its data-backing badge)

- The same PMMA fire with a ceiling detector and vents on is first detected after 132.5 s on Earth, 187.5 s on Mars and 253.5 s on the Moon, and not within 300 s at 0 g.

- On dust-only events, a two-moment detector raised no false alarms, versus 5.6% for a single-measurement detector.

- With vents off at 0 g, the flame does not spread at all, consistent with BASS-II's low-flow limit: the ventilation dilemma.

These rely partly on assumed mixing and detector constants, and EMBER labels them that way.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Engineers get a ranked list of fire blind spots and countermeasures before hardware exists. Researchers get a map of conditions no experiment has covered, such as solid-fuel flame spread above 21% oxygen and anything at partial gravity, which shows where future experiments like those planned for partial gravity are most needed. The same approach applies on Earth to oxygen-enriched or low-airflow spaces such as hospital oxygen-therapy wards, submarines, aircraft cargo holds and mines.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

EMBER treats fire safety as an adversarial game, with one agent trying to defeat the habitat's detection while another defends it. It also treats honesty about data as a feature: every number shows how much real NASA data backs it, and the interface refuses to call partial-gravity results "measured".

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, and pycma (CMA-ES) for the backend; React, three.js with React Three Fiber, and Vite for the frontend. Optional Claude API in the app for scenario ideas and answer phrasing. Hosted on Vercel (frontend) and Render (backend).

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

We kept limitations visible. Partial-gravity results are always labeled interpolated because PSI has no partial-g data. Suppression limits from FLEX are droplet-scale, so applying them to a whole cabin is labeled extrapolation. The Ghost Flame Auditor makes no claim for solids or outside FLEX's tested range. In our runs, Red's search does not yet beat random search with the same budget, and we report that rather than hide it.
